titre: Peirce and the Four Ways of Believing
accroche: In 1877, an American logician sorts every way of ending doubt into four families, from the most comfortable to the most demanding.
contenu_vulgarise:
Doubt is uncomfortable, belief is a form of rest. Between the two, Charles Sanders Peirce writes in 1877 in “The Fixation of Belief,” published in the magazine Popular Science Monthly, there are only four possible paths, and only one of them guarantees that people will not all go wrong together in the same direction.

## Four methods

The first, the method of tenacity, consists in choosing a belief and sticking to it by avoiding anything that might contradict it. Peirce notes that it “is really pursued by many men,” and that it brings real peace of mind, as long as no one else interferes: it collapses on first contact with a neighbor who believes the opposite with the same confidence.

The second, the method of authority, hands belief over to an institution, religious or political, which imposes a doctrine and represses deviations. Peirce judges it more stable, since it erases contradiction by forbidding it: “let the will of the state act, then, instead of that of the individual.” It too fails once an individual notices that other societies, under other authorities, believe the opposite just as firmly.

The third, the a priori method, picks whatever seems reasonable, “agreeable to reason.” But what each person finds reasonable depends on their era and taste, not on experience: Peirce compares it to a fashion, one that changes from century to century without ever converging on a stable agreement.

What remains is the scientific method, which assumes that things have real characters, “entirely independent of our opinions about them,” and relies on experience to discover them. It is the only one of the four, Peirce writes, where any man, given enough experience and reasoning, will be led to the one true conclusion.

## What this shifts

The shift is not to say that science is right and the other three are wrong: the first three methods each bring a real relief from doubt, and Peirce does not treat them as crude reasoning errors. What sets them apart is that they fix a belief without guaranteeing anything about how the world would respond if consulted: they can collapse at the first disagreement, since nothing in them plans for what to do with one. The scientific method is the only one that plans for its own revision, and that alone, in Peirce's eyes, is what makes it superior, not some moral superiority of those who practice it.

carte.punch: In 1877, a logician sorts every way of ending doubt into four families.
carte.idee: Charles Sanders Peirce distinguishes four methods for fixing belief in 1877: tenacity, authority, a priori reason, and the scientific method. The first three settle doubt without guaranteeing anything in the face of disagreement; only the last anticipates its own revision.

quiz.question: Why is the scientific method, according to Peirce, superior to the other three ways of fixing belief?
choix: Because it is practiced by a majority of recognized scholars
Because it alone plans for what to do with disagreement, instead of collapsing before it
Because it alone brings real relief from doubt
Because it was imposed by an international scientific authority
quiz.explication: The first three methods also bring real relief from doubt, and the scientific method owes nothing to any authority or to a number of practitioners: what sets it apart, Peirce says, is that it plans for its own revision in the face of disagreement, while the others collapse as soon as one arises.
